title: Can We Just Opt Out?
author: Stephen Fitzpatrick
source: Teaching in the Age of AI (fitzyhistory.substack.com), November 2, 2026
summary: Stephen Fitzpatrick, a history teacher, uses a veteran colleague's plea to 'opt out' of email in the 1990s as a lens on a University of Kentucky administrator who won a religious exemption from using AI at work. He argues that the exemption is unlikely to be repeatable at scale because administrative functions at schools and universities behave like businesses with every incentive to adopt AI for efficiency. Classroom AI practice, protected by professional autonomy and real pedagogical concerns, will probably stay optional far longer than the administrative layer, just as email changed the infrastructure of the job without changing how teachers taught. He notes that schools are practiced at accommodation, and he offers students an opt-out from his own classroom AI experiments, but wonders whether the same generosity will reach adults once AI is woven into reporting, communication, learning management systems and grade books. The piece closes with the uncertainty of the next four years, including what today's seniors will face in the job market, and the humbling admission that he misjudged how long teachers could avoid AI entirely.
points: The Kentucky exemption was granted only because the employee was never required to use AI; the university explicitly said accommodations may be reviewed as job functions evolve.
Administrative work (admissions, advancement, scheduling, HR) is where AI adoption will become hardest to refuse, while classroom practice remains the most protected zone.
The email analogy is the central argument: a technology that did not change how teachers taught still reshaped the job's infrastructure and made opting out impossible.
Schools routinely accommodate students on technology (laptops for some, screen exemptions for others), which raises the question of whether adults will receive equal generosity.
Whether teachers can still avoid AI by 2030 is an open question the author admits he got wrong in 2023.
quotes: After close to forty years in a world where he was insulated from a daily barrage of interruptions, he was asking if he could continue without these intrusions in the twilight of his teaching life. Nearly thirty years later, present-day me sympathizes with those very prescient concerns. Of course, he did not get to opt out. None of us did.
You have to have ownership of your cognitive processes and your ability to determine your path to the world and abdicating that, or even parts of that, lessens the person.

The administrative side of a school or university operates more like a business. Admissions, advancement, scheduling, and HR are all being offered AI tools in the name of efficiency, and institutions trying to manage their bottom lines more aggressively have every incentive to use them.

Professional autonomy and the very real pedagogical concerns around learning make it likely that classroom AI practice will remain the most protected part of the job for much longer. Email didn’t change how we taught, but it did change the administrative infrastructure of how the job is done and all the ancillary requirements surrounding it.

Schools are, if anything, more practiced at accommodation than most workplaces. As a teacher currently, and selectively, experimenting with AI in the classroom, I will always provide an opt-out for students who are uncomfortable with the technology.

We have gone from clunky chatbots in early 2023 to AI agents that can take on real chunks of white-collar work, solve advanced math and physics problems, and write competent software from plain-English instructions as we near the end of 2026.
Despite the significant penetration of AI into society overall, a large number of people have never used one. Many teachers still want nothing to do with AI.
If you had asked me in early 2023 whether teachers would still be able to avoid AI entirely by the fall of 2026, I would have said no. I was clearly wrong.
